title: What the Client Asked For vs. What They Need
description: Havenmark wants a quick homepage check before a board meeting. The real exposure is somewhere else entirely — and scoping the audit correctly is the first skill of running a real one.

learningObjectives.text: Distinguish a client's stated request from the audit scope they actually need, and justify the difference
Sample pages by template and state variant rather than testing exhaustively or by traffic alone

contentSections.body: Havenmark's IT director emails you: "Can you run a quick accessibility check on our homepage before the board meeting Thursday?" Nothing else. You already know two things she didn't mention: the European Accessibility Act's compliance deadline has already passed, and a wheelchair user's advocacy group filed a formal complaint two weeks ago that the checkout flow is unusable with a screen reader. The homepage looks fine at a glance. It's also almost certainly not where the company's actual exposure is sitting.

This is the first judgment call of a real audit, and it happens before you open a single dev tool: **the request you're given and the scope you actually need are frequently two different things**, and the gap between them is exactly where a junior audit goes wrong.

A client's stated request usually reflects what's visible to them — the page they look at most, the thing a board member asked about, the flow named in a complaint. It rarely reflects where the actual accessibility risk and legal exposure concentrate, because if the client already knew that, they wouldn't need an outside audit. Your job in the first conversation is to take the stated request seriously as information about what the client cares about, then scope the engagement around what the evidence in front of you (a live complaint, an EAA deadline, transaction-critical flows) actually points to.

That doesn't mean overriding the client silently. It means naming the gap out loud: "You asked for the homepage. Given the checkout complaint and the EAA deadline, here's what I'd recommend scoping instead, and why." A client under real regulatory pressure generally wants that conversation — the ones who don't are telling you something too.

contentSections.question: Before reading on: if you only had time to audit one thing at Havenmark this week, would it be the homepage the client asked for, or the checkout flow named in the complaint? Why?
contentSections.answer: Checkout — but the more precise answer is neither in isolation. The complaint tells you checkout is a confirmed, active risk, which makes it the obvious priority for available time. But a one-off checkout audit doesn't establish the company's actual EAA conformance picture, which is what the board meeting and the legal pressure are really about. A scoped, honest answer names checkout as priority one while being explicit that a single flow isn't the same thing as a site-wide audit.
contentSections.hint: Ask which one tells you about a confirmed, already-active risk, versus which one was simply the easiest thing for the client to name.

contentSections.scenario: You're deciding how to sample Havenmark's ~14,000 product pages, all built from one template with in-stock, out-of-stock, and on-sale variants. Some sampling logic genuinely reflects where distinct barriers live. Some just sounds rigorous.
contentSections.question: Select every basis that correctly justifies which pages to include in the sample.

items.label: Each distinct template state (in-stock, out-of-stock, on-sale) — different markup, different potential barriers
Whether the page sits inside the required purchase journey (browse, cart, checkout, account)
Whether the page contains a custom interactive widget not seen elsewhere (like the color-swatch filter)
A statistically random sample of a fixed percentage of all pages
Whichever pages the client's marketing team wants reviewed first

explanation.template-variant: Applicable. Two pages sharing a template share the same underlying markup and the same barriers — sampling by state variant is what actually finds the differences that matter, like a missing announcement on an out-of-stock badge.
explanation.journey-step: Applicable. A page's place in the required purchase sequence determines whether a barrier on it can block the whole transaction — that's a structural reason to include it, independent of how many people see it.
explanation.distinct-widget: Applicable. A custom-built control (the swatch filter, the accordion) carries its own risk profile that a generic template page doesn't — it needs its own sample entry regardless of how it's classified elsewhere.
explanation.traffic-rank: Not applicable as the sampling basis. Traffic tells you how many people are exposed, which matters for later prioritization, not which pages structurally differ enough to need independent testing.
explanation.random-sample-size: Not applicable. A random sample of near-identical template instances mostly retests the same markup repeatedly, at the cost of the budget that should go toward covering genuinely distinct templates and journey steps.
explanation.client-preference: Not applicable as the sole basis. What the client wants reviewed is useful input into the conversation about scope — the same conversation as the homepage-versus-checkout question — but it isn't, on its own, a technical justification for sample coverage.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the six are about what's structurally different or structurally load-bearing on the page; the other three are about volume, randomness, or preference. Sampling logic has to answer "where would a barrier be different here," not "where do the most people go" — those are different questions with different right answers.

contentSections.body: Scope the audit around the client's actual risk, not just the words in their request — and say the gap between the two out loud rather than silently overriding it. Sample pages by template variant and by position in the critical purchase journey, not by traffic or by testing everything.

title: Building the Test Environment Matrix
description: "Just test in Chrome" is not a test environment. Deciding — and writing down — exactly which browsers, screen readers, and OS versions the audit covers is what makes every finding in the report reproducible.

learningObjectives.text: Justify a browser/AT/OS test matrix against a client's real user base rather than convenience
Explain why the test environment matrix must be explicitly stated in the audit report

contentSections.body: You send Havenmark a scoping document listing the browsers and screen readers you'll test with. Their lead developer replies: "Can we simplify this? Just test in Chrome — that's what we use internally, and it'll save you time." It would save time. It would also tell you almost nothing about whether the site works for the actual disabled customers Havenmark has, because none of them chose their assistive technology based on what the internal dev team happens to run.

The test environment matrix is a decision you make once, early, and write down — not something that emerges from whatever happens to be open on your machine that day. It has three dimensions that all move independently:

**Browser.** Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge — each has different levels of ARIA support and different quirks in how it exposes the accessibility tree.

**Assistive technology.** NVDA and JAWS on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS/iOS, TalkBack on Android — and these aren't interchangeable with each other or evenly matched to browsers. VoiceOver is built for and best supported in Safari; testing it in Chrome risks surfacing bugs that are really about that mismatch, not about Havenmark's code.

**Operating system and version.** Screen reader behavior can shift across OS updates and AT versions — an NVDA release from two years ago doesn't always announce a live region the same way the current one does.

The matrix you choose should reflect the client's real user base — their actual traffic mix across desktop and mobile, the AT combinations known to be common among their users or their user category generally — not auditor convenience and not the client's internal tooling. And once decided, it goes in the report, explicitly, because a finding without a stated environment can't be reproduced, and an area you didn't test can't be honestly implied to have passed.

contentSections.question: Havenmark is majority Windows desktop with growing mobile share. Before reading the exercise below, guess: which single AT/browser pairing would be the worst one to skip entirely?
contentSections.answer: There isn't one uniquely safe answer, which is the point — NVDA+Chrome, JAWS+Chrome, VoiceOver+Safari, and TalkBack+Chrome each cover a genuinely distinct population that the others don't. Skipping mobile (TalkBack) entirely is a particularly common and risky omission, since it's the one desktop-focused teams most often forget, even as mobile share grows.
contentSections.hint: Ask which pairing covers a user group none of the others reach at all.

contentSections.code:
Draft scoping email to Havenmark:

"Test environment: we'll verify the site using the latest version of NVDA on the latest version of Chrome on Windows 11. This covers screen reader testing for the engagement."
contentSections.question: This scoping email will be included as the environment statement in the final report. What's the flaw in stopping here?

options.label: A single browser/AT/OS combination doesn't reflect the real spread of how Havenmark's customers actually access the site — VoiceOver/Safari users and mobile TalkBack users are silently left untested
"Latest version" is too casual a phrase and should be replaced with a formal legal disclaimer
NVDA isn't a legitimate screen reader to test with at all

feedback.single-combo-incomplete: Correct. One combination, however well-chosen, silently narrows the audit's real coverage far below what the report's "screen reader testing" language implies — VoiceOver, Safari, iOS, and Android AT users are all left completely untested, with nothing in this statement to flag that gap to the reader.
feedback.latest-version-vague: Wrong target. "Latest version" pinned at the actual test date is a legitimate way to record a version — the real problem is coverage breadth, not the precision of the version phrasing (though pinning the literal version number, e.g. "NVDA 2025.2," is still better practice for future reproducibility).
feedback.nvda-not-real: False — NVDA is a widely used, entirely legitimate free screen reader and a correct choice to include. The flaw is that it's the *only* one included, not that it was included at all.

contentSections.flawExplanation: The email reads as a complete environment statement while actually describing a fraction of the real matrix — exactly the failure this lesson exists to prevent. A statement this narrow, dropped unchanged into the final report, would imply broader coverage than the audit performed, leaving Havenmark with false confidence about their VoiceOver, Safari, and mobile AT users specifically.

contentSections.body: Decide the browser, AT, and OS matrix from the client's real user base before you start testing — not from convenience — and put the exact matrix in the report. It's what makes every finding reproducible and what honestly bounds what the audit actually covered.

title: Running axe, WAVE, and Lighthouse — and Knowing What They Missed
description: An automated scan on Havenmark's product listing comes back nearly clean. The filter sidebar underneath it is completely unusable by keyboard, and the scan has no way to know that.

learningObjectives.text: Explain what automated accessibility scanners can and cannot structurally detect, and why
Use an automated scan as triage before manual testing, without treating a clean result as a stopping point

contentSections.body: You run axe DevTools against Havenmark's product listing page. Three violations come back: two color-contrast instances, one missing image alt. Everything else is green — including the filter sidebar, where the color-swatch "checkboxes" are actually plain <div> elements with click handlers, no role, no keyboard handler, and no tabindex. A mouse user clicks them and filters the results. A keyboard user tabs straight past every one of them without ever knowing they exist. The scan doesn't know either.

The scan isn't wrong about what it checked — it's silent about what it can't check, and the gap between those two things is the whole reason this audit needs a human.

**What axe, WAVE, and Lighthouse genuinely catch well:** missing alt attributes, insufficient color contrast against a computed ratio, missing form labels with no association at all, duplicate IDs, missing document language, empty links and buttons, and a meaningful set of structural ARIA misuse patterns — all of it detectable by reading the DOM and computed styles, with no need to interact with the page.

**What none of them can catch, structurally:** whether a click handler has a matching keydown handler, where keyboard focus actually goes after a Tab press, whether a visible focus indicator exists, what a screen reader actually announces landing on a control, whether alt text is *meaningful* rather than merely present, and whether a page is usable at all versus merely markup-clean. These aren't gaps in any one tool's ruleset that a better or newer tool will eventually close — they require executing an interaction and observing the result, which is categorically different from scanning a static DOM.

The three tools also overlap more than teams expect: WAVE and Lighthouse's accessibility audits are both largely built on rule sets similar to axe-core's. Running all three buys you some redundancy and a slightly different presentation of the same core findings — it does not buy you keyboard or AT coverage. That only comes from picking up a keyboard yourself, which is where the rest of this module goes next.

contentSections.question: Before you read the exercise: the axe scan on the filter sidebar shows zero violations. What specifically would a scan have to be able to do, that it currently can't, to catch the broken swatch checkboxes?
contentSections.answer: It would have to actually simulate pressing Tab, observe whether focus lands on the element, and simulate a keypress to see whether anything responds — a live interaction and observation loop, not a read of the DOM's static properties. That's a fundamentally different kind of check than anything a scan-and-report tool performs.
contentSections.hint: Ask what "press Tab and see what happens" requires that "read the markup" doesn't.

contentSections.scenario:
WAVE flags an "Alert" (not an error) on an empty

used purely as a visual spacer, and shows a green checkmark for "Alt text present" on the hero banner image, whose actual markup is alt="banner_hero_v3_final.jpg".
contentSections.question: Which of these is the case where the tool's pass is actively misleading, rather than just incomplete?

options.label: The alt text — it's marked green because a string is present, but that string is a filename a screen reader will read aloud verbatim, meaningless to a blind user
The empty heading — WAVE's Alert here is a false alarm and can be dismissed without checking
Neither is a real issue, since WAVE didn't report either one as a hard error

feedback.alt-filename: Correct. "Does alt exist" and "is alt meaningful" are different checks, and WAVE can only automate the first — the green checkmark actively signals "fine" on exactly the thing that isn't. The empty heading, by contrast, was correctly surfaced as something to check, not silently passed.
feedback.empty-heading-false-alarm: Backwards — an Alert flags something for human judgment precisely because it's often a real problem; an empty heading used as a spacer is a genuine, common barrier for anyone navigating by heading list, one of the most frequent screen reader navigation patterns.
feedback.neither-real: Wrong — the empty heading is a real, reportable defect (WAVE just didn't call it a hard error), and the alt text's green pass is the one actively producing false confidence, which is the more dangerous of the two.

contentSections.mechanism: A presence check ("is there a value in this attribute") and a quality check ("is that value meaningful to the person hearing it") are structurally different kinds of test. Automated tools can only run the first reliably — the moment quality or intent matters, the result requires a human to actually read what the tool found and judge it, which is exactly what turns a scan result into an audit finding.

contentSections.body: Run the automated scan first — it's fast, cheap triage that clears a real category of static defects before you spend expensive manual time. Never treat a clean scan as a stopping point: it can't execute a keyboard interaction, can't judge whether text is meaningful, and can't tell you the page is usable, only that it's markup-clean on the narrow slice it checks.

title: The Keyboard Pass: Filters, Cart, and the Focus That Went Nowhere
description: A systematic, page-by-page keyboard pass through Havenmark's filter sidebar finds three separate defects an automated scan missed entirely — and none of them are about missing labels.

learningObjectives.text: Run a systematic keyboard pass across a critical journey and identify focus-visibility, focus-management, and state-communication defects
Distinguish keyboard operability from focus visibility from ARIA state communication as three separate, separately testable requirements

contentSections.body: Mouse aside. You're tabbing through Havenmark's filter sidebar the way any keyboard-only user would. You reach a color swatch and press Tab again — and the visible focus indicator vanishes entirely. Nothing on the page shows where you are. DevTools confirms document.activeElement is still the swatch; the browser knows exactly where focus is. You, looking at the screen, don't. That's finding one, and you haven't even checked a filter yet.

The keyboard pass is the first manual test in the sequence, and it's methodical rather than exploratory: go through each critical-journey page in order, mouse aside, and check the same handful of things at every interactive element.

**Is focus visible?** SC 2.4.7. A control being reachable in the tab order and a sighted keyboard user being able to see where they are are two separate facts — CSS `outline: none` with nothing substituted breaks the second while leaving the first intact, exactly like the swatch above.

**Is the tab order logical?** Does it follow reading order, or does it jump unpredictably because of a CSS reorder or a misplaced DOM node?

**Are there traps?** Does Tab (and Shift+Tab) ever get stuck somewhere, unable to continue?

**Do custom widgets follow their expected pattern?** An accordion, a combobox, a listbox each have an established interaction pattern (from the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices) — Enter/Space to toggle, correct state communicated via ARIA attributes, and for some patterns, arrow-key navigation between related items.

**What happens to focus after a dynamic update?** This is the one a scan will never catch and a junior auditor often misses: when JavaScript re-renders part of the page — a re-filtered product grid, a re-opened panel — where does keyboard focus land afterward? If the answer is "back at the top of the document," that's a defect, even if every individual control involved is perfectly labeled and operable in isolation.

contentSections.question: You check a filter checkbox and the product grid re-renders via AJAX with no page reload. Before reading on: where would focus land in a correctly-built version of this interaction?
contentSections.answer: On or near the control the user just activated — often the checkbox itself, or a sensible nearby point like a heading announcing the updated result count — not reset to the top of the document. The point is that the user shouldn't have to rebuild their position in the page from scratch after every single filter they apply.
contentSections.hint: Ask what a well-built interaction owes the user immediately after their own action changes the page.

contentSections.question: You're running the keyboard pass on the filter sidebar for the first time. Put these steps in the order that actually surfaces all three classes of defect — visibility, trap, and dynamic-update focus loss.
steps: Put the mouse aside entirely before starting
Tab through every control in the sidebar once, noting anything with no visible focus indicator
Tab past the last control and confirm focus continues into the next page region rather than getting stuck
Activate one filter checkbox and observe exactly where focus lands after the grid updates
Repeat the activation step for a second filter, to confirm the first result wasn't a one-off
contentSections.explanation: The order matters because each step isolates a different class of defect, and doing them out of order lets one mask another. Visibility has to be checked first, on every control, while you're still moving in a predictable straight line — it's easy to miss a single silent control if you're also trying to track trap or focus-loss behavior at the same time. Checking for a trap comes next, at the natural end of the tab sequence, before anything gets activated and changes the DOM. Only after both of those are confirmed clean do you actually activate a control and watch focus — because activating something reshapes the DOM, and you want your baseline observations about visibility and trapping done against the original, unmodified markup. Repeating the activation step matters because a single observation could be a fluke of that particular checkbox; a second one confirms it's the interaction pattern itself, not a one-off, which is what turns an observation into a reportable, reproducible finding.

contentSections.body: The keyboard pass checks four separate things at every control — visible focus, logical order, no traps, and correct state communication on custom widgets — plus one thing a scan will never find: where focus goes after a dynamic update. A control can pass every one of the first four and still lose the user completely on the fifth.

title: The Screen Reader Pass: What NVDA Says at Checkout That axe Never Flagged
description: A required checkout field fails validation. Visually, the error is obvious. With NVDA running, focused on the exact field that's broken, nothing about the error is announced at all.

learningObjectives.text: Run a structured AT pass across a critical journey, checking announcements at each interactive element against expected behavior
Diagnose whether a missing or incorrect AT announcement stems from missing association, missing live-region markup, or a responsive layout difference

contentSections.body: Checkout, card number field, left blank on purpose. You submit. NVDA announces "Form submission failed. 3 errors," reading from a summary heading at the top of the form — a genuinely good pattern, present and working. You tab down to the card number input itself, the exact field that's broken, and NVDA says: "Card number, edit text." That's it. No error. No indication anything is wrong with the specific field you're sitting on. A sighted user staring at the same field sees a red border and the words "This field is required" six pixels below it.

The AT pass follows the same journey as the keyboard pass, but the question at every stop changes: not just "can I reach and operate this," but **"what does the screen reader actually say when I do, and does that match what a sighted user sees or experiences?"**

A few categories come up constantly in a real audit:

**Error association.** An error summary at the top of a form is good practice — it gives an AT user a fast overview. But it doesn't substitute for per-field association: without `aria-describedby` pointing the input at its specific error text (or `aria-invalid="true"`), focusing the broken field re-announces only its name and role, never the reason it failed, every single time the user returns to it.

**Status messages.** Havenmark's "Added to cart" toast is visually obvious and completely silent to VoiceOver, because a plain, unmarked `<div>` gives assistive tech no signal that new content appeared. A `role="status"` (or an equivalent `aria-live="polite"`) region fixes this without stealing focus from whatever the user was doing — which matters, because the fix isn't "move focus here," it's "announce this without interrupting."

**Divergence across AT and platform.** The same order-history table can announce cleanly with JAWS on desktop and fall apart with TalkBack on mobile — often because the responsive layout genuinely restructures the DOM at a narrow viewport, not because either screen reader is malfunctioning. When two AT/browser pairings disagree sharply on "the same page," the first move is checking whether the DOM is actually the same at both breakpoints, not distrusting one of the tools.

And throughout: what gets written down is the **verbatim announcement** — the literal string, or its precise absence — not a paraphrase. "NVDA didn't say anything" and "NVDA said the wrong thing" point to genuinely different fixes, and a developer can't tell which one they're looking at from a summary.

contentSections.question: The card number field's visual error text exists and looks correctly placed. Before reading the exercise: what's the most likely single attribute missing from the markup that would explain NVDA staying silent when focus lands on the field?
contentSections.answer: A missing aria-describedby on the input pointing at the id of the error text element (often paired with a missing aria-invalid="true"). The error text itself is probably fine and visible — it's just not programmatically wired to the specific field, so nothing tells the screen reader to read it when that field receives focus.
contentSections.hint: The error text exists and is visible — the missing piece is the programmatic link between the field and that text, not the text itself.

contentSections.scenario: Order-history table, 40 rows. JAWS + Chrome on desktop: table navigation announces "row 3 of 40, order number, date, status, total" cleanly. TalkBack + Chrome on the same page on mobile: swiping produces a fragmented, out-of-order jumble — dates and totals with no clear structure.
contentSections.question: What's the correct next investigative step, before writing this up as a finding?

options.label: Check whether the table's DOM structure actually differs at the mobile breakpoint, not just re-run TalkBack
Conclude TalkBack has a bug and drop it from the environment matrix going forward
Rate it low severity immediately, since JAWS on desktop handles it correctly

feedback.check-dom-at-breakpoint: Correct. Many responsive layouts restructure a data table into stacked divs, or reorder cells with CSS, at narrow viewports — checking the actual DOM at the mobile breakpoint tells you whether this is a genuine markup defect (fixable, reportable, with a clear cause) or something else entirely, and that answer changes both the fix and the severity you'd assign.
feedback.exclude-talkback: This is the trap the whole domain warns against — distrusting a legitimate, widely-used AT the moment it surfaces something confusing, instead of treating that confusion as evidence to investigate.
feedback.rate-low-desktop-fine: Jumps to severity before the investigation is finished, and assumes desktop coverage is what matters — checking order history from a phone is a common, real task, and the cause hasn't even been established yet.

contentSections.concept: When two AT/browser/platform pairings diverge sharply on what looks like "the same page," the first question is whether it's actually the same DOM at both points, not which tool to distrust. Responsive design frequently changes markup structure at breakpoints for visual reasons that have nothing to do with — and everything to do with breaking — the underlying table semantics a screen reader relies on.

contentSections.body: The AT pass asks what's actually announced at every stop in the journey, not just whether a control is reachable. Write down the verbatim announcement or its precise absence — it's the difference between a developer knowing to add a live region and a developer guessing at what's wrong.

title: Cognitive Load and Content: The Pass No Automated Tool Can Run
description: Havenmark's checkout times out silently after 10 minutes, and a failed payment shows nothing but an error code. Neither one trips a single automated check — and both are real, citable WCAG failures.

learningObjectives.text: Identify cognitive and content-quality barriers against specific WCAG success criteria where they exist
Recognize and honestly name real usability barriers that fall outside a specific WCAG criterion, rather than forcing an ill-fitting citation

contentSections.body: Ten minutes into filling out Havenmark's checkout form, with no warning of any kind, the session expires. The page redirects to a generic error, and the cart — every item, all of it — is empty. No countdown appeared. No "your session is about to expire" prompt. Nothing in this failed a single automated scan, because nothing about it is a missing label or a contrast ratio. It's a person, mid-task, silently timed out of buying something.

This pass has no tool to run and no keyboard sequence to follow. It's a close read of the content and interaction design itself, against the parts of WCAG that cover comprehension, time, and predictability rather than markup.

**Timing.** A silent 10-minute checkout timeout with no way to extend it is SC 2.2.1 Timing Adjustable — content with a time limit has to let the user turn it off, extend it, or adjust it (narrow exceptions apply, like real-time auctions). This isn't abstract: for someone who needs more time to read, decide, or physically complete input, a silent cutoff isn't an inconvenience, it can make the task structurally impossible to finish, every single time.

**Error content.** "Error 402: Payment validation failed. Ref: PMT-VAL-0043" identifies the problem to an engineering log, not to the person standing in front of it trying to buy something. SC 3.3.1 Error Identification and SC 3.3.3 Error Suggestion both cover this — an error has to be described in terms a person can act on, and this barrier hits everyone, not only AT users, though it compounds for anyone already spending more effort to get through the page.

**Sensory-only instructions.** "Choose the size in the green box" fails SC 1.3.3 Sensory Characteristics the moment the only way to identify the recommended option is a color — a colorblind user, a screen reader user, or someone in high-contrast mode can't act on it, no matter how good the contrast on that green actually is.

And some real problems genuinely don't map cleanly onto one WCAG number — a 12-section filter panel with no active-filter summary and no "clear all" is a real cognitive burden that WCAG's specific criteria only partially cover. The honest move, when that happens, is to say so directly in the finding rather than force a citation that doesn't quite fit. That's not a weaker finding — forcing the wrong number is what actually weakens a report's credibility.

contentSections.question: The 10-minute checkout timeout has no visible countdown and no warning. Before the exercise: which WCAG principle is this really about — perceivable, operable, understandable, or robust — and why?
contentSections.answer: Operable. Timing Adjustable (SC 2.2.1) sits under the Operable principle because a time limit that can't be extended removes the user's ability to operate the interface on their own terms — it's not about whether the content can be perceived or understood, it's about whether the person is given enough control over time to actually complete the interaction.
contentSections.hint: Ask which of the four principles is fundamentally about the user having control over how the interface behaves, not about the content itself being legible or clear.

contentSections.body: This pass has no scan and no keyboard shortcut — it's reading the content and timing decisions the way a person under time pressure or cognitive load would experience them, and citing the specific criterion when one genuinely fits (2.2.1 for timing, 3.3.1/3.3.3 for errors, 1.3.3 for sensory-only instructions) — and saying plainly when a real problem doesn't map to one.

title: Writing a Finding a Developer Can Reproduce — and Rating It Honestly
description: Two auditors write up the same bug. One writeup gets fixed by end of day. The other gets a Slack message asking what page it was even on. Then: rating severity by what a barrier actually blocks, not by how easy it looks to fix.

learningObjectives.text: Write a finding with reproducible steps, expected vs. actual results, verbatim AT output, element, and cited criterion
Rate severity by user impact and blocking-ness rather than ease of fix, prevalence, or proximity to other findings

contentSections.body: Same bug, two writeups. Auditor A: "Checkboxes in filter sidebar are not accessible. Fails WCAG." Auditor B: "Steps: 1) Go to /category/lighting 2) Tab into filter sidebar 3) Tab to first color-swatch checkbox. Expected: NVDA announces the color name and checked state. Actual: NVDA announces 'clickable' only — no label, no role, no state (NVDA 2025.2 + Chrome 127). Element: div.filter-swatch[data-color='navy']. WCAG 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A)." One of these gets fixed today. The other gets a reply asking which page, which browser, and what "not accessible" is even supposed to mean.

Everything found in the last four lessons is only as useful as how it's written up. A real finding has five parts, every time:

**Steps to reproduce.** Exact navigation, exact interaction, in order — enough that someone who's never seen the bug can walk it themselves.

**Expected vs. actual.** What should have happened, stated plainly, against what actually happened.

**Environment.** The specific browser, AT, and version combination that produced this result — tied directly back to the matrix from lesson two.

**The specific element.** A selector, an id, something a developer can go find in the codebase without guessing.

**The cited criterion.** The WCAG success criterion this violates, which frames severity, gives the finding a shared vocabulary, and lets the client's team map it against their own compliance obligations.

Then comes the second half of the skill, which is where junior audits go wrong even when the writeup itself is solid: **severity is rated by user impact and blocking-ness — can the affected user complete the task at all, or not — never by how easy the fix looks, how common the bug category is, or how small the affected population seems.** An unlabeled submit button that fully blocks a purchase for every screen reader user who reaches it is Critical regardless of whether the fix is a one-line `aria-label`. A missing focus-visible outline on a control that remains reachable and operable is real, but it isn't the same severity as a total block — mixing those two up either way, in either direction, is what breaks a report's usefulness.

And when a client pushes back with "how many people does this actually affect" — as one eventually will — the answer isn't to go find better statistics. It's that a complete blocker stays a complete blocker for whoever hits it, and "keyboard-only" or "screen reader user" almost always undercounts the real affected population anyway, since switch access, voice control, and plenty of temporary situations rely on the exact same underlying mechanics.

contentSections.question: Before the exercises: name, in one sentence, the actual difference between a Critical and a Serious finding, using "blocking" rather than "bad."
contentSections.answer: Critical fully blocks a task for the affected user group — they cannot complete it at all, by any means, using the interface as built. Serious significantly degrades the experience or blocks a specific sub-task without blocking the entire transaction. The line is whether the door is closed, or just much harder to open.
contentSections.hint: Ask, for each severity level, whether the user can still finish the task some other way, or whether they're stopped entirely.

contentSections.scenario: You're triaging four findings from the Havenmark audit and assigning each one a severity. Some reasoning genuinely tracks impact. Some sounds like it does but is actually tracking something else.
contentSections.question: Select every basis that correctly belongs in a severity decision.

items.label: Whether the affected user can complete the relevant task at all, by any means, using the interface as built
Whether the barrier blocks a single sub-task or the entire transaction end to end
That the true affected population is usually broader than the narrowest label (e.g. "keyboard-only" also includes switch access and voice control)
How much developer time the fix is estimated to take
How common this category of bug is across the industry
Whether a formal complaint has already been filed about this specific issue

explanation.can-complete-task: Applicable. This is the core test — a total block, regardless of how many people encounter it, is what earns the highest severities.
explanation.scope-of-blocking: Applicable. A barrier that stops one sub-task differs meaningfully from one that stops the entire transaction, and severity should reflect that difference honestly.
explanation.real-population-includes-more: Applicable. Narrow labels like "keyboard-only" routinely undercount who's actually affected, since the same underlying mechanics serve switch access, voice control, and temporary situations too — correcting for that is part of an honest severity judgment.
explanation.fix-effort: Not applicable to severity. Ease of fix is a legitimate input into remediation *sequencing*, but folding it into the severity rating itself is exactly how genuinely blocking bugs get quietly deprioritized for being inconvenient to fix.
explanation.bug-commonness: Not applicable. How typical a bug category is speaks to how likely it is to be noticed or complained about, not to how much it actually blocks the specific user in front of it.
explanation.complaint-filed: Not applicable as a severity basis, though it's a legitimate reason to prioritize *investigating* something sooner. A barrier doesn't become more or less blocking because someone has or hasn't already complained about it.

contentSections.synthesis: Three of the six describe the barrier's actual effect on the user; three describe something adjacent — cost, familiarity, or visibility to outsiders — that feels relevant but answers a different question. Keeping severity locked to impact is what makes the rating trustworthy enough for a client to actually prioritize against.

contentSections.body: A finding needs steps, expected vs. actual, environment, element, and cited criterion — enough for someone who's never seen the bug to reproduce it and fix it without a follow-up meeting. Severity tracks whether the user can complete the task at all, never how easy the fix looks or how small the affected population seems.

title: Retesting, False Positives, and Delivering the Audit
description: A verified fix introduces a new bug. An automated flag turns out to be wrong. A filter panel passes every single check and is still nearly unusable. This lesson closes the Havenmark engagement with the full audit report.

learningObjectives.text: Retest a fix against its original finding while remaining alert to regressions the fix may have introduced
Distinguish a genuine automated-tool false positive from a real finding, and identify conformant-but-unusable patterns conformance testing alone would miss
Produce a complete audit report — scope, methodology, environment matrix, findings, and severity — as a real deliverable

contentSections.body: The developer fixes the unlabeled "Place order" button by adding aria-label="Place order". You retest with NVDA+Chrome — the button announces correctly now, exactly as expected. You keep going, because a retest isn't finished the moment the original bug is confirmed fixed: submitting the form now moves focus to a hidden "processing" spinner with no accessible name of its own, and NVDA announces just "group" while the page underneath goes inert. The fix worked. It also broke something that wasn't broken yesterday.

Three judgment calls close out a real audit, and all three require the same instinct: don't stop at the first plausible answer.

**Retesting.** Verify the original finding using the same AT/browser combination that produced it — not a different, more convenient one — because that's the only way to confirm the actual reported behavior actually changed. Then keep testing nearby. Fixes to focus and DOM behavior are exactly where regressions like the silent spinner above tend to appear, precisely because the fix itself touched focus management. A regression gets its own finding, with its own severity — it doesn't reopen the original, which is genuinely resolved.

**False positives.** Automated tools flag real conditions, computed correctly, sometimes against the wrong threshold. A "Sale −20%" badge at 24px bold flagged at 3.8:1 contrast looks like a violation against the default 4.5:1 minimum — until you notice 24px bold qualifies as large text under SC 1.4.3, where the real minimum is 3:1, and the worst-case point across the badge's gradient clears that. The tool wasn't lying; it was applying the wrong bar. Verifying this by hand, rather than reporting the raw flag, is exactly the judgment a checklist can't supply on its own — and it's worth a documented note in the report either way, not a silent drop.

**Conformant but unusable.** A filter panel can pass every single criterion you individually test — labeled controls, visible focus, logical order, correct ARIA state, announced updates — and still take 40-plus keyboard actions to do what a mouse does in 6 clicks. Nothing in that sentence is a WCAG violation you can point to by number. It's still a real, reportable barrier, grounded in a concrete, countable comparison rather than forced under a criterion it doesn't actually violate — forcing the wrong citation here costs the report's credibility with anyone who checks it and finds the cited criterion genuinely fine.

Then the deliverable itself: everything from scoping through severity across product listing, filters, cart, checkout, and account converges into one document — the audit report, with its own brief, its own rubric, and a worked example below of what a complete one actually looks like.

contentSections.question: The spinner bug appeared only after the button-label fix shipped. Before the exercise: should it be filed as part of the original finding, or as something new?
contentSections.answer: Something new. The original finding — no accessible name on the button — is genuinely, verifiably resolved. The spinner is a distinct defect that didn't exist before this change and needs its own steps, environment, and severity; folding it into the old finding's status obscures that this is a regression from the fix, not a failure of it.
contentSections.hint: Ask whether the thing originally reported is now true or false — separately from whether anything else changed.

contentSections.body: **The domain artefact.** Everything below is a complete, real-shaped deliverable: a client brief, the rubric a senior reviewer would grade it against, and a full worked exemplar — the actual Havenmark audit report this domain has been building toward, lesson by lesson.

contentSections.intro: Before the worked exemplar, assemble the report's own structure. Four decisions about what a complete audit report has to contain.

fields.prompt: What comes first in the report, right after the title?

options.label: Scope and methodology — what was tested, why, and the environment matrix
options.value: scope and methodology, including the stated environment matrix

options.label: The full list of findings, most severe first
An executive summary praising what the site already gets right

fields.correctValue: scope and methodology, including the stated environment matrix

feedback.scope and methodology, including the sta: Right — a reader deciding how much to trust the findings needs to know what was actually tested and how, before seeing a single result. This is the paragraph lesson two's environment-matrix principle turns into.
feedback.the full findings list: Findings without a stated scope and environment leave the reader unable to judge what wasn't tested, or reproduce anything — this has to come after, not instead of, the methodology.
feedback.an executive summary of positives: A audit report isn't a marketing document. Leading with positives before scope and methodology risks framing the whole report as reassurance rather than an honest account of what was found.

fields.prompt: How should each individual finding be structured in the report?

options.label: Steps to reproduce, expected vs. actual, environment, element, criterion, severity
options.value: steps, expected vs actual, environment, element, criterion, severity

options.label: A one-line description and a WCAG number
options.value: one-line description and a criterion number

options.label: A screenshot with a red circle around the problem

fields.correctValue: steps, expected vs actual, environment, element, criterion, severity

feedback.steps, expected vs actual, environment,: Right — this is the full reproducible-finding structure from lesson seven, and it's what turns a report into something a developer can act on without a follow-up meeting.
feedback.one-line description and a criterion num: This is Auditor A's writeup from lesson seven — technically points at a real WCAG criterion but gives a developer nothing to reproduce or verify against.
feedback.an annotated screenshot only: Useful as supporting evidence, especially for visual issues like the contrast badge — but on its own it can't capture what a screen reader announced, and it's not a substitute for written reproduction steps.

fields.prompt: What should severity in the report be rated against?

options.label: User impact and blocking-ness
Estimated developer hours to fix
How many other findings are similar to it

feedback.user impact and blocking-ness: Right — this is the standard from lesson seven, and it's what lets the client trust the severity column enough to actually prioritize against it.
feedback.estimated fix effort: This is the conflation the domain warns against directly — folding ease of fix into severity is how genuinely blocking bugs quietly slip down the priority list for being inconvenient.
feedback.similarity to other findings: Grouping similar findings is a reasonable organizational choice for the report's structure, but it isn't a basis for rating any individual finding's severity.

fields.prompt: What should close the report, after the findings?

options.label: A summary that separates genuine conformance gaps from conformant-but-unusable patterns, stated honestly as two different categories
options.value: a summary distinguishing conformance gaps from usability-only findings

options.label: A single overall pass/fail verdict for the whole site
Nothing — the findings list is the whole report

fields.correctValue: a summary distinguishing conformance gaps from usability-only findings

feedback.a summary distinguishing conformance gap: Right — this is exactly the conformance-versus-accessibility distinction from this lesson: some findings are clean WCAG violations, and some (like the 40-actions filter panel) are real barriers that don't map to a criterion number, and a report that's honest about which is which is more credible, not less.
feedback.a single pass/fail verdict: A single verdict flattens exactly the nuance this whole domain has been building — a site can conform on paper and still be unusable in a specific, real, countable way; collapsing that into one word erases the distinction.
feedback.no closing section: Leaving the findings unsynthesized makes the client do the work of figuring out what it all means for their EAA exposure and their roadmap — which is a large part of what they're paying an auditor, not just a scanner, to do.

contentSections.synthesis: Scope and methodology first, fully reproducible findings in the middle rated by impact, and an honest closing synthesis that doesn't flatten conformance and usability into the same thing. That's the shape of the exemplar that follows.

contentSections.body:
**THE BRIEF**

Havenmark (mid-size EU homeware retailer, EU-wide shipping) has engaged you for a full accessibility audit ahead of European Accessibility Act enforcement, triggered in part by a formal complaint that checkout is unusable with a screen reader. Deliver a report covering: scope and methodology, the test environment matrix, findings with severity, and a closing synthesis — in a form Havenmark's engineering lead can hand directly to their development team.

---

**THE RUBRIC**

A passing report:

1. States scope as template samples plus the full critical purchase journey, with the reasoning named, not just the page list.
2. States the exact environment matrix (browser + AT + OS versions) and any explicit exclusions — nothing implied by silence.
3. Every finding has steps to reproduce, expected vs. actual, environment, specific element, cited WCAG criterion (or an honest note where none cleanly fits), and severity rated strictly by user impact and blocking-ness.
4. Includes at least one finding that's a genuine WCAG citation and at least one that's a documented false-positive resolution or a conformant-but-unusable judgment call — showing the range of judgment a checklist alone can't produce.
5. Closes with an honest synthesis distinguishing conformance gaps from usability-only findings, rather than a single flattened verdict.

---

**WORKED EXEMPLAR — Havenmark Accessibility Audit (excerpt)**

**1. Scope and Methodology**

This audit covers a representative sample of Havenmark's site rather than an exhaustive page-by-page review: the homepage; the category-listing template; the product-detail template across its in-stock, out-of-stock, and on-sale state variants; the custom filter sidebar (color swatches, price range, category accordion); cart; the three-step checkout (address, payment, confirmation); and account login, registration, and order history. This sample was chosen because pages sharing a template share the same underlying markup and barriers, and because the critical purchase journey — the sequence a customer must complete unassisted to buy something — determines where a single barrier can block an entire transaction, independent of that page's individual traffic volume. Deep account-settings sub-pages beyond login, registration, and order history were excluded from this pass by agreement with the client, given the majority-guest-checkout usage pattern (78% of orders); this exclusion is stated here explicitly rather than left implicit.

**2. Test Environment Matrix**

NVDA 2025.2 + Chrome 127 (Windows 11); JAWS 2025 + Chrome 127 (Windows 11); VoiceOver + Safari (macOS Sequoia, desktop) and VoiceOver + Safari (iOS 18, physical device); TalkBack + Chrome (Android 14, physical device). Manual keyboard testing performed independent of AT, mouse aside, across all sampled pages. Automated scanning performed with axe DevTools, WAVE, and Lighthouse as a first-pass triage layer, not as a substitute for the manual and AT passes above.

**3. Findings (representative selection)**

**Finding 1 — Filter sidebar color-swatch controls are not keyboard operable.** *Steps:* Navigate to any category page; tab into the filter sidebar; attempt to reach a color swatch. *Expected:* Swatch receives keyboard focus and can be toggled with Space or Enter. *Actual:* Swatch is a `<div>` with a click handler only — no `tabindex`, no `role`, no keydown handler; it is entirely skipped by Tab. *Environment:* Confirmed keyboard-only, all browsers; automated scan (axe) reported zero violations on this element. *Element:* `div.filter-swatch[data-color]`. *Criterion:* SC 2.1.1 Keyboard (A). *Severity:* Critical — this filter dimension is completely unusable by any keyboard-only or switch-access user; the automated scan's silence on this exact element is noted explicitly as a methodology caution.

**Finding 2 — Checkout "Place order" button has no accessible name.** *Steps:* Reach the final checkout step; tab to the submit button. *Expected:* NVDA announces "Place order, button." *Actual:* NVDA announces "button" only. *Environment:* NVDA 2025.2 + Chrome 127. *Element:* `button#submit-order` (icon-only, no text content, no aria-label). *Criterion:* SC 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value (A). *Severity:* Critical — screen reader users cannot identify which control completes the purchase; this is the button named in the client's original complaint.

**Finding 3 — Payment iframe traps keyboard focus.** *Steps:* Tab into the embedded payment fields; continue pressing Tab. *Expected:* Focus exits the iframe after its last field and reaches "Place order." *Actual:* Focus cycles indefinitely within the iframe. *Environment:* Keyboard-only, confirmed across all tested browsers; third-party payment processor iframe — remediation will require vendor engagement, flagged here explicitly. *Criterion:* SC 2.1.2 No Keyboard Trap (A). *Severity:* Critical — total block on completing any purchase for keyboard-only users.

**Finding 4 — "Added to cart" toast is not announced.** *Environment:* VoiceOver + Safari, both desktop and iOS. *Actual:* No announcement; confirmation only available by manually checking the cart icon. *Criterion:* SC 4.1.3 Status Messages (AA). *Severity:* Serious — task remains completable, but confirmation is entirely lost for VoiceOver users, degrading trust in whether the action succeeded.

**Finding 5 (verification note, not a defect) — "Sale −20%" badge contrast.** axe flagged 3.8:1 against a 4.5:1 default threshold. Manual verification: badge text is 24px bold, qualifying as large text under SC 1.4.3, where the applicable minimum is 3:1; worst-case measured contrast across the gradient background is 3.2:1, which clears the correct threshold. Documented here as a resolved false positive, not carried forward as a finding.

**Finding 6 (usability, no single clean citation) — Filter panel combined interaction cost.** Every individual criterion tested on the filter panel passes — labeled controls, visible focus, correct `aria-expanded`, announced grid updates. Applying three filters from a fresh page load requires expanding three independently collapsible sections and roughly 40 keyboard actions total, against 6 mouse clicks for the same result, with no "clear all" or persistent active-filter summary available at any point. *Severity:* Serious, on usability-cost grounds rather than a specific WCAG citation — noted honestly as such rather than forced under SC 2.4.3, which the panel's actual focus order does not violate.

**4. Closing Synthesis**

Of the findings in this audit, three (Findings 1–3) are direct, unambiguous WCAG conformance failures blocking core transaction steps and should be treated as the immediate remediation priority ahead of any EAA enforcement action. One (Finding 4) is a conformance gap with a clear fix and moderate — not total — impact. One (Finding 5) demonstrates why automated scan output requires manual verification before being reported as a defect. One (Finding 6) illustrates the gap this audit was specifically commissioned to catch: a pattern that is fully WCAG-conformant by every individual criterion tested, and still meaningfully harder to use than its mouse equivalent — the category of barrier a checklist-only review would have reported as clean.

Retest with the same environment that produced the finding, and keep testing after the fix confirms — regressions hide in exactly the code a fix just touched. Verify an automated flag before reporting it, and report a conformant-but-unusable pattern honestly even when no single WCAG number fits. The report itself is the artefact: stated scope, stated environment, reproducible findings rated by impact, and a synthesis that doesn't flatten conformance into accessibility.
